answer.evidence: The tile is a plan view looking down a ramp. Rows 1-10 are the snow terrace top, ending in a darker edge line at row 11. Rows 12-29 are the beige ramp surface, with horizontal step lines at rows 12, 18-19 and 24. Dark cut-wall strips run along both side edges. Only the 2 pale rows at 30-31 could pass for a front lip. There is no vertical south face of 3 or more rows, so the whole tile is one horizontal or sloped surface seen from above.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are fine on paper: 7 visible tones per tile (paving reference 7, grass reference 3), 3% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outline is tinted blue-grey rather than black. By eye the piece is weaker. It is a pale, low-contrast snow ramp with only about 4 soft lightness bands. Only 9 distinct colours are used in total, against 80 for the grass reference. There are no per-clump highlights, snow grain or crust speckle, and no visible shading of the cut walls beyond a faint gradient. The darker rim around the whole patch makes it read as a boxed 'sticker' or bucket shape, not a tileable ground surface with Beodeul-style material texture. It looks thinner and flatter than either reference, so I fail it.
